sections.title: Presenting symptoms, functional class and chest pain

blocks.text: Heart disease produces a short list of symptoms, so screen for each one: **chest pain or discomfort**, **breathlessness** (on exertion, orthopnoea, PND), **ankle swelling**, **palpitations**, **syncope**, **intermittent claudication** and **fatigue**. A close link between symptoms and exertion is the hallmark of cardiac disease.

blocks.title: NYHA functional classes (breathlessness); CCS uses the same four grades for angina
rows: No limitation: ordinary activity causes no symptoms
Slight limitation: comfortable at rest, ordinary activity brings on symptoms
Marked limitation: comfortable at rest, but less-than-ordinary activity brings on symptoms
Symptoms with any physical activity, and possibly at rest

blocks.title: Chest pain: pattern points to the cause
rows: Central tightness or heaviness; may spread to jaw or arms
Predictably brought on by exertion or emotion; settles with rest or GTN within minutes
Similar ischaemic pain but more severe
Starts at rest, lasts longer (over ~30 min favours ACS over stable angina); sweating, nausea, breathlessness, faintness
Maximal at the moment of onset, goes through to the back; interscapular pain = descending aorta; hypertension, Marfan, Ehlers–Danlos
Worse lying flat, eased by sitting up and leaning forward
Worse with deep breath or cough; not exertional
Worse lying flat or after meals; spasm may ease with nitrates or warm drinks
Moves with breathing or shoulder movement; reproduced by pressing on the spot

blocks.title: ESC classification of chest pain (count the features)
items: Feature 1: retrosternal discomfort of typical quality and duration
Feature 2: provoked by exertion or emotional stress
Feature 3: relieved by rest and/or GTN
**All three** = typical angina; **two** = atypical angina; **one or none** = non-cardiac chest pain

blocks.title: Taking the chest pain history
items: Ask about chest **discomfort** rather than pain: angina is often a dull ache or pressure
Ischaemic pain is usually central and may radiate to the jaw or arms; it very rarely goes below the umbilicus
The most useful features are **reproducibility, predictability and the link with exertion**
Note how long the symptom has been present: **recent-onset angina** carries more risk than long-standing stable symptoms
Pain lasting days without a break is unlikely to be angina or ACS

blocks.title: History features that raise the likelihood of ACS (positive LR)
rows: Radiation to the right arm or shoulder

blocks.title: First investigations suggested by the history
items: **Exertional chest pain:** FBC, fasting glucose, lipids, thyroid function and a 12-lead ECG. A normal exercise ECG cannot rule out coronary disease; if suspicion remains, CT coronary angiography. Echo if a murmur is heard
**Suspected ACS:** a 12-lead ECG is mandatory and, with troponin I or T, is the main triage tool. If the first troponin is normal, repeat it 6–12 hours after symptom onset or admission

blocks.text: Radiation to the **right** arm or to both arms raises the likelihood of ACS more than radiation to the left arm.

Prompt relief with sublingual GTN does **not** prove angina: oesophageal spasm also responds and the placebo effect is strong. Angina that now comes with less effort or at rest is unstable, i.e. an ACS.
Ischaemia may be painless: **diabetic** patients are prone to silent infarcts, and heart-transplant recipients may feel no angina because the heart is denervated.
Angina mimics: reflux can give angina-like pain without heartburn and can coexist with angina; cholecystitis gives RUQ tenderness; herpes zoster pain can come before the rash appears.

blocks.note: Look at: the hand gestures patients use for ischaemic pain (clenched fist, flat hand) and its usual radiation to jaw and arms
Look at: where angina is felt and where it radiates

sections.title: Breathlessness, oedema, palpitations, syncope and claudication

blocks.title: Cardiac breathlessness
items: Usually **chronic and exertional**: LV output cannot rise with exercise, so LV end-diastolic and pulmonary venous pressures climb, fluid enters the interstitium and the lungs stiffen
Sudden onset suggests MI, acute pulmonary oedema or acute mitral regurgitation (e.g. ruptured chorda)
**Orthopnoea:** breathless lying flat; ask how many pillows the patient needs
**PND:** wakes from sleep gasping, often with cough and wheeze; sits on the edge of the bed or opens a window; settles over minutes. Sleep blunts awareness, so oedema builds up before waking
Cheyne–Stokes breathing can occur in severe heart failure

blocks.title: Heart or lung?
rows: Cough and wheeze as leading symptoms

blocks.text: If there is **no orthopnoea**, LV failure is very unlikely to explain the breathlessness (negative LR 0.047). Orthopnoea is a feature of **left**-sided failure.

blocks.title: Non-cardiac causes of orthopnoea
items: Massive ascites
Pregnancy
Bilateral diaphragm paralysis
Large pleural effusion
Severe pneumonia

blocks.title: Ankle swelling
items: Cardiac oedema is **symmetrical, painless, pitting and dependent**
It builds through the day, is worst in the **evening** and improves overnight; bed-bound patients collect it over the **sacrum**
Recent weight gain (3 kg or more) may be noticed
Ask about **calcium-channel blockers**, which cause ankle oedema
Facial puffiness points to nephrotic syndrome rather than heart failure

blocks.title: Palpitations: description and likely rhythm
rows: A pause, then a single forceful thump ("missed beats")
Very fast and regular; starts and stops abruptly; ended by vagal manoeuvres; polyuria afterwards
Regular, pounding, 90–120/min, builds and settles gradually
Sinus tachycardia: anxiety or a hyperdynamic state (anaemia, pregnancy, thyrotoxicosis, AR)
Fast, with syncope, or in a patient with heart failure or old MI
Slow, heavy beats (often not felt at all)

blocks.title: Palpitation history and next steps
items: Continuous or in discrete attacks? Regular or irregular? Rate? Abrupt or gradual onset and offset?
Ask the patient to **tap out** the rhythm
Triggers (exercise, caffeine, alcohol); associated chest pain, light-headedness, pre-syncope or syncope; known structural heart disease
Arrhythmias switch on and off suddenly; sinus tachycardia speeds up and slows down gradually
Record an ECG **during** an episode (ambulatory or patient-activated recorder). Palpitations with pre-syncope or syncope need prompt investigation; most other cases are benign
Carotid sinus massage can end SVT but risks stroke if there is carotid disease

blocks.title: Syncope (transient loss of consciousness from cerebral hypoperfusion)
rows: Young; emotional or postural trigger; warning of nausea, sweating, yawning, tinnitus, dizziness; quick recovery lying flat
On standing or after meals; drugs; autonomic neuropathy
On **exertion**: aortic stenosis, HCM (also pulmonary stenosis, PE, atrial myxoma)
Sudden collapse with no warning; pale, slow or absent pulse; flushes on recovery
No warning; known heart disease; family history of sudden death; sick sinus syndrome alternates fast and slow rhythms
Aura, tongue biting, jerking, incontinence, drowsy or confused afterwards

blocks.title: Drug causes of syncope
items: **QT prolongation:** flecainide, sotalol, amiodarone, quinidine, domperidone, erythromycin or clarithromycin, haloperidol
**Bradycardia:** β-blockers, verapamil, diltiazem, digoxin
**Postural hypotension:** most antihypertensives (especially prazosin and calcium-channel blockers) and anti-Parkinsonian drugs

blocks.title: Claudication and fatigue
items: **Claudication:** calf, thigh or buttock pain after a fairly fixed walking distance, relieved by standing still. Pain at rest means severe ischaemia
Acute limb ischaemia, the six Ps: pain, pallor, pulselessness, paraesthesia, perishingly cold, paralysis
**Fatigue** in heart failure reflects poor perfusion, but also think of poor sleep, β-blocker side effects, diuretic-induced electrolyte upset, and infection such as endocarditis

blocks.text: Spinal stenosis gives pseudo-claudication that eases only on sitting or bending forward, not by simply standing still.
A prolonged Stokes–Adams attack can cause a fit from cerebral hypoxia and be mislabelled epilepsy. Always get an **eyewitness** account and ask about family sudden death (long QT, Brugada).

blocks.note: Look at: the palpitation algorithm, which splits by regularity and by discrete attacks over 120/min

sections.title: Risk factors, past, drug, family and social history

blocks.title: Coronary risk factors to record
items: **Known coronary disease** (the strongest predictor), then hypercholesterolaemia
Smoking, recorded in **pack-years**
Hypertension and diabetes: duration and control
Family history of premature coronary disease in a **first-degree relative before age 60**
Chronic kidney disease; rheumatoid or other chronic inflammatory disease
Obesity, inactivity, male sex, older age, erectile dysfunction
Cocaine or amphetamine use (an important cause of MI in young people)

blocks.title: Lipid numbers in the history
rows: Total cholesterol below 4 mmol/L; LDL 1.8 mmol/L or less

blocks.text: After stopping smoking, the risk of **MI** falls to that of a never-smoker in about **2 years**; the risk of developing angina takes about **10 years** to approach non-smoker levels.

A diabetic with no known coronary disease has roughly the same MI risk as a non-diabetic who has already had an infarct. In CKD, coronary disease is the commonest cause of death on dialysis. Erectile dysfunction is a sensitive marker of vascular disease.

blocks.title: Past and treatment history
items: Previous angioplasty or CABG
Rheumatic fever clues: childhood "growing pains", long bed rest, regular penicillin injections, chorea; it predisposes to **valve disease**
Dental decay matters in valve disease because of endocarditis risk
Hypertension: salt, weight, alcohol, exercise, home readings, past and present drugs and side effects, NSAIDs or steroids, kidney symptoms
Heart failure: fluid restriction (often about 1500 mL/day) and daily weights

blocks.title: Family and social history
items: Early heart disease in relatives suggests a genetic cause such as familial hypercholesterolaemia
Sudden death in the family suggests HCM, long QT or Brugada syndrome
Social: capacity to work, stairs and adaptations at home, cardiac rehabilitation, baseline function and level of care

blocks.text: A family history only "counts" as a coronary risk factor when a **first-degree** relative was affected **before 60**. A grandparent or uncle, or an MI at 70, does not qualify.

sections.title: General inspection, hands, pulse and blood pressure

blocks.title: Order of the examination
items: Expose the chest and sit the patient at **45°** (also the position for the JVP)
General appearance: breathlessness, posture, cyanosis, pallor, Marfanoid build
Hands → radial pulses → blood pressure → face and mouth → neck (JVP, carotids) → praecordium
Then lung bases, sacrum, abdomen and legs (oedema, peripheral pulses)

blocks.title: Peripheral signs and what they mean
rows: Cyanotic congenital heart disease (especially Fallot) or infective endocarditis (about 10% of subacute IE)
Usually trauma, but endocarditis is an important cause
Tender red nodules on the finger pulps: endocarditis
Painless macules on palms or pulps: endocarditis
Can be normal; xanthelasma may go with type II/III; arcus adds some risk
Severe congestive failure or haemolysis from a prosthetic valve

blocks.title: Cyanosis
items: Visible once capillary oxygen saturation falls below about **85%**
**Central:** right-to-left shunt (Fallot, transposition) or acute pulmonary oedema; look at tongue and lips
**Peripheral:** cold hands and feet from vasoconstriction or stasis (heart failure, shock, cold, Raynaud)
Left-to-right shunts do not cause central cyanosis

blocks.title: Rate and rhythm
items: Normal resting rate is usually quoted as 60–100/min; bradycardia below 60, tachycardia above 100
**AF:** irregularly irregular in time and volume; stays irregular after exercise, whereas ectopic beats often disappear
**Pulse deficit:** in AF or frequent ectopics the apical rate exceeds the radial rate because short-filled beats are too weak to reach the wrist
**Sinus arrhythmia:** rate rises on inspiration; normal
A regular rate of about 150 suggests atrial flutter with 2:1 block; fever adds 15–20 beats/min per °C
**Radiofemoral delay** (especially in a young hypertensive) suggests coarctation; unequal radial pulses suggest subclavian stenosis or aortic dissection

blocks.title: Pulse character (feel the carotid or brachial)
rows: Aortic regurgitation, PDA, hyperdynamic states (anaemia, sepsis), AV fistula
Mixed aortic stenosis and regurgitation; HCM
Bigeminus (every sinus beat followed by an ectopic)
Sepsis, hypovolaemic shock, after aortic valve replacement
Tamponade, severe asthma, less often constrictive pericarditis

blocks.title: Measuring blood pressure
items: Standard cuff bladder width is 12.5 cm; a normal cuff on a large arm **overestimates** BP
Avoid an arm with a dialysis fistula
Find the palpated systolic first, then auscultate with the arm at heart level, deflating 3–4 mmHg per second
Systolic = **Korotkoff I**; diastolic = **Korotkoff V** (disappearance). Use phase IV (muffling) in severe AR or when sounds never disappear
Beware the **auscultatory gap** (phase II silence) being mistaken for diastolic
Arms may differ by up to 10 mmHg; leg pressure is up to 20 mmHg higher than arm pressure except in coarctation

blocks.text: **Pulsus paradoxus** is a misnomer: it is an exaggeration of the normal inspiratory fall in systolic BP, to **more than 10 mmHg**. Think tamponade, severe asthma and constriction; aortic regurgitation is not a cause.

Books define **postural hypotension** differently. Talley uses a fall of over 15 mmHg systolic or 10 diastolic after a minute standing; Kumar uses 20 mmHg systolic. Learn **Davidson's**: a drop of **more than 20 mmHg systolic or 10 mmHg diastolic** on standing from lying. Drugs are the commonest cause.

blocks.note: Look at: bigeminy, trigeminy, couplets, sinus arrhythmia and the irregularly irregular pulse of AF
Look at: slow-rising, collapsing, alternans, bisferiens and dicrotic waveforms against the normal pulse
Look at: the Korotkoff phases, with systolic at the first sound and diastolic at disappearance

sections.title: Neck and praecordium: JVP, apex, heaves and thrills

blocks.title: Assessing the JVP
items: Use the **internal jugular**: it is in direct continuity with the SVC and right atrium, so its height reflects right atrial pressure
Patient at **45°**, head supported and turned slightly left; look along sternocleidomastoid
Measure the vertical height above the **sternal angle**; more than **3 cm** means raised right-heart filling pressure
High in right heart failure and fluid overload; **low in hypovolaemia**
If hard to see, firm pressure over the abdomen makes it rise

blocks.title: Venous or arterial pulsation?
rows: Two peaks per cycle (in sinus rhythm)
Falls on inspiration; changes with posture
Barely palpable; abolished by light pressure at the root of the neck
Easily palpable; not occluded by light pressure

blocks.title: JVP waveform
rows: Right atrial contraction (just before the carotid pulse)
Atrial filling against a closed tricuspid valve during ventricular systole
Tricuspid opening and rapid ventricular filling

blocks.title: Abnormal JVP findings
rows: Complete heart block; VT with AV dissociation
Pulmonary hypertension, pulmonary stenosis, tricuspid stenosis
Heart failure, fluid overload, renal salt and water retention, SVC obstruction

blocks.text: **Abdominojugular test:** press firmly over the upper abdomen for 10 seconds. A rise that stays above 4 cm suggests RV failure or a raised left atrial pressure.

blocks.title: Apex beat
items: Davidson: normally in the **5th or 6th intercostal space at the mid-clavicular line**
Count spaces down from the sternal angle (the 2nd space lies just below it)
Felt in only about half of adults; may be impalpable with obesity, emphysema, pericardial or pleural effusion
LV dilatation moves it **down and laterally**

blocks.title: Apex character
rows: Mitral or aortic regurgitation, dilated cardiomyopathy
LV aneurysm or LV dysfunction after anterior MI

blocks.title: Rest of the praecordium
items: **Left parasternal heave** (heel of the hand): RV hypertrophy or severe LA enlargement
**Palpable P2:** severe pulmonary hypertension
**Thrills** usually mean a severe valve lesion (e.g. a basal thrill in AS). Feel apical thrills with the patient on the left side, basal thrills sitting forward in full expiration
**Scars:** median sternotomy = valve surgery or CABG (look for leg vein-harvest scars); a lateral thoracotomy under the breast = old closed mitral valvotomy
Pacemaker or ICD box below the clavicle; a box eroding through the skin is serious because of infection

blocks.text: Mitral stenosis does not enlarge the LV, so the tapping apex is **not displaced**.
Normal apex position: Talley places it 1 cm medial to the mid-clavicular line in the 5th space; Davidson says the **5th or 6th space at the mid-clavicular line**. Use Davidson's wording in the exam.

blocks.note: Look at: the patient at 45° with the sternal angle, JVP height and mid-right atrium lined up
Look at: a, c, x, v and y timed against S1 and S2
Look at: JVP waveforms in TR (giant v), constriction (steep y), pulmonary hypertension (large a) and tricuspid stenosis

sections.title: Auscultation technique, heart sounds and added sounds

blocks.title: Technique
items: Areas: **aortic** 2nd right ICS at the sternal edge; **pulmonary** 2nd left ICS; **tricuspid** lower left sternal edge; **mitral** the apex
**Bell** (lightly) for low-pitched sounds: S3, S4, the mid-diastolic rumble of MS
**Diaphragm** for high-pitched sounds: S1, S2, systolic murmurs, AR, clicks, opening snap
Time everything against the **carotid pulse**: S1 comes just before the upstroke; systolic murmurs coincide with it
Left-sided sounds are louder in expiration, right-sided in inspiration

blocks.title: Heart sounds
rows: Mitral stenosis (mobile valve), tachycardia or hyperdynamic circulation, short PR
First-degree block, mitral regurgitation, heart failure, LBBB, heavily calcified MS
Loud in hypertension; soft in calcific aortic stenosis
Delayed RV emptying: RBBB, pulmonary stenosis
Delayed LV emptying: LBBB, severe AS
Physiological in the young and in pregnancy; pathological in heart failure and MR
Stiff ventricle: AS, hypertension, HCM. Never present in AF

blocks.title: Added sounds
rows: Mitral stenosis; moves closer to S2 as stenosis worsens; lost if the valve calcifies
Mobile congenital aortic or pulmonary stenosis
Mechanical prosthetic valve (replaces S1 for mitral, S2 for aortic)
Scratching, up to three components, varies with posture and breathing; best sitting forward in expiration

blocks.title: Normal effects of inspiration
items: JVP falls
Systolic BP falls by up to 10 mmHg
Heart rate rises
S2 splits: P2 is delayed and A2 comes slightly earlier

blocks.text: An S3 is the most useful cardiac sign of LV failure, together with a displaced apex. A **new S3 after MI** predicts death (LR+ 8.0).
Do not call every S3 pathological. Davidson lists S3 as **normal in young people and pregnancy**; it is the S4 that always means disease.
In mitral stenosis S1 is **loud**; a soft S1 is the trap answer. The opening snap belongs to MS, not to pulmonary hypertension.

blocks.note: Look at: the cardiac cycle with S1–S4, clicks and the opening snap lined up against the ECG

sections.title: Murmurs, dynamic manoeuvres and completing the examination

blocks.title: Murmurs by timing
rows: Aortic stenosis or sclerosis, pulmonary stenosis, HCM, ASD flow, innocent flow murmur
Mitral valve prolapse, papillary muscle dysfunction
Mitral stenosis, tricuspid stenosis, increased flow, Austin Flint (AR)

blocks.title: Murmur intensity (Davidson)
rows: Very soft; heard only in ideal conditions
Audible without the stethoscope on the chest

blocks.title: Describing a murmur (SCRIPT)
items: **S**ite where loudest; **C**haracter (blowing, rasping, rumbling); **R**adiation (AS to the carotids, MR to the axilla)
**I**ntensity (grade); **P**itch; **T**iming in the cycle
Radiation only happens with a high-velocity jet

blocks.title: Classic murmurs
rows: Slow-rising pulse, narrow pulse pressure, soft A2, basal thrill, heaving apex
Soft S1, S3, displaced thrusting apex
Pansystolic, harsh, lower left sternal edge
Soft early diastolic at left sternal edge, sitting forward in held expiration
Collapsing pulse, wide pulse pressure; Austin Flint rumble at the apex
Low mid-diastolic rumble at the apex, bell, left lateral
Loud S1, opening snap, tapping apex, malar flush

blocks.title: Dynamic manoeuvres
rows: HCM louder; AS and MR softer
HCM softer; AS and MR louder
MR and VSD louder; HCM softer
Left lateral position, bell at apex
Brings out AR and a pericardial rub

blocks.text: **Innocent murmur:** soft, mid-systolic, at the left sternal edge, no radiation, and the rest of the heart is normal. Benign murmurs are **never diastolic**. A systolic murmur that radiates or has a thrill is almost always pathological (a systolic thrill has LR+ 12).

Davidson says MR, TR and VSD are the **only** causes of a pansystolic murmur (Talley adds rare aortopulmonary shunts). Kumar allows a grade 4 murmur without a thrill; Davidson ties grade 4 to a thrill. Follow Davidson.

blocks.title: Completing the examination
items: Lung bases: crackles, effusion
Sacral and ankle oedema; peripheral pulses
Abdomen: tender hepatomegaly (pulsatile in TR), ascites, splenomegaly (endocarditis), expansile aorta (AAA)
Heart failure signs to collect: tachycardia, raised JVP, displaced apex, S3/S4, bibasal crackles, effusion, oedema, ascites, tender liver
In hypertension add radiofemoral delay, BP in both arms (over 10 mmHg difference suggests vascular disease), postural BP, fundi, renal bruits and urine for blood

blocks.text: A carotid bruit is a poor predictor of significant stenosis, and the AS murmur always carries to the neck. A venous hum vanishes with light pressure over the neck.

blocks.note: Look at: pansystolic, ejection systolic, late systolic, early diastolic and mid-diastolic murmur shapes
Look at: where each murmur is loudest and where it radiates
Look at: the four auscultation areas on the chest wall

cards.front: ESC chest pain classification: how many features make "typical angina"?
cards.back: All three: typical retrosternal discomfort, provoked by exertion or emotion, relieved by rest or GTN. Two = atypical; one or none = non-cardiac.

cards.front: NYHA class III?
cards.back: Comfortable at rest, but less-than-ordinary activity causes symptoms (marked limitation).

cards.front: Chest pain: tearing, maximal at onset, through to the back?
Which radiation of chest pain has the highest LR+ for ACS?
Negative LR of absent orthopnoea for LV failure?
cards.back: 0.047: no orthopnoea makes LVF very unlikely.

cards.front: Palpitations ended by Valsalva, with polyuria afterwards?
Sudden collapse without warning, pale, then flushing on recovery?
Family history of CAD: which relatives and age count?
After quitting smoking, when does MI risk match a never-smoker?
Postural hypotension (Davidson)?
cards.back: Fall of more than 20 mmHg systolic or 10 mmHg diastolic on standing from lying.

cards.front: Pulsus paradoxus threshold and causes?
cards.back: Inspiratory systolic fall over 10 mmHg: tamponade, severe asthma, constrictive pericarditis.

cards.front: Bisferiens pulse?
cards.back: Mixed aortic stenosis and regurgitation, or HCM.

cards.front: Cannon a waves?
cards.back: Complete heart block, or VT with AV dissociation.

cards.front: Normal apex position (Davidson)?
Tapping apex beat?
Fixed wide splitting of S2?
Which added sound is never heard in AF?
Only causes of a pansystolic murmur (Davidson)?
HCM murmur with Valsalva and squatting?
cards.back: Louder with Valsalva strain, softer on squatting (opposite to AS and MR).

cards.front: Murmur grade 4 (Davidson)?

questions.leadIn: Pick the best match from the list for each case below. Any option can serve several cases, or none at all.

items.stem: A 57-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension develops sudden, extremely severe pain between his shoulder blades while lifting a box. He says it felt as if something ripped, and it was at its worst the instant it started.
items.explanation: Pain that is **maximal at onset**, described as tearing and felt **between the scapulae** points to dissection of the descending aorta; hypertension is the risk factor.

items.stem: A 64-year-old woman has had chest tightness when walking uphill for two months, easing after a few minutes of rest. Yesterday the same tightness came on while she sat watching television and lasted 15 minutes. ECG and two troponin measurements 8 hours apart are normal.
items.explanation: Step 1: the pattern has changed from exertional to **rest pain**, which is unstable. Step 2: normal serial troponins separate unstable angina from infarction.

items.stem: A 31-year-old man had a flu-like illness last week. Now he has sharp central chest pain that is worse when he lies back and on deep breathing, and better when he sits up and leans forward.
items.explanation: Sharp, pleuritic central pain that is **worse lying flat and eased by leaning forward** after a viral illness is pericarditis.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman describes a retrosternal pressure lasting about five minutes. It comes on when she climbs stairs or argues with her son. It does not settle with rest, and a GTN spray prescribed by her GP has never helped.
questions.leadIn: Using the ESC three-feature classification, how is her pain best classed?
questions.explanation: Count the features: typical retrosternal discomfort (yes), provoked by exertion or emotion (yes), relieved by rest or GTN (**no**). Two of three features = **atypical angina**.
whyNot: Typical angina needs all three features, including relief by rest or GTN.
Non-cardiac pain has one feature or none; she has two.
Unstable angina is a change in pattern (rest pain, less effort); this pain is still exertional.
Brief, exertion-provoked episodes of five minutes are not the prolonged rest pain of infarction.

questions.theme: Causes of transient loss of consciousness
questions.leadIn: Pick the best match from the list for each case below. Any option can serve several cases, or none at all.

items.stem: A 19-year-old student faints while giving blood. Just before, she felt hot, sick and sweaty and kept yawning. She came round within a minute of being laid flat.
items.explanation: A young patient, an emotional trigger, a **prodrome** of nausea, sweating and yawning, and quick recovery lying flat: vasovagal.

items.stem: A 79-year-old man slumps in his chair mid-sentence with no warning. His wife says he went grey and she could not feel a pulse. Within half a minute he came round and his face flushed bright red.
items.explanation: No warning, pallor with an absent pulse, then **flushing on recovery** is the classic Stokes–Adams attack from complete heart block.

items.stem: A 73-year-old man collapses while walking briskly up a hill. He has had tightness in his chest on exertion for some months. His carotid pulse rises slowly and is of small volume.
items.explanation: Step 1: **exertional** syncope means an obstructive cause (AS or HCM). Step 2: a **slow-rising, small-volume** pulse identifies aortic stenosis.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman has episodes of a very fast, regular heartbeat. Each one starts suddenly with a "flip" and stops just as suddenly, sometimes when she holds her breath and strains. Afterwards she passes large amounts of urine.
questions.leadIn: Which rhythm is most likely?
questions.explanation: Fast, **regular**, abrupt on and off, stopped by a vagal manoeuvre (Valsalva), with **polyuria** afterwards: SVT.
whyNot: AF feels fast and irregular, and is not reliably ended by Valsalva.
Sinus tachycardia builds up and settles gradually rather than switching on and off.
Ectopics feel like a pause then a single thump, not sustained racing.
VT is suggested by syncope or known structural heart disease; a well young woman ending attacks with Valsalva fits SVT.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman has a murmur. She remembers months of bed rest as a child because of painful, swollen joints, and monthly penicillin injections throughout her teens.
questions.leadIn: This history mainly raises the likelihood of which condition?
questions.explanation: Long childhood bed rest, joint pains and **regular penicillin prophylaxis** are clues to past **rheumatic fever**, which leads to valve disease.
whyNot: HCM is genetic; the clue is a family history of sudden death, not childhood rheumatic illness.
Coarctation is congenital and suggested by radiofemoral delay and hypertension.
FH is suggested by early coronary disease in relatives and xanthomata.
Brugada is suggested by a family history of sudden death.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man attends for a cardiovascular risk review. He gives several details about his relatives.
questions.leadIn: Which detail counts as a significant family history of coronary disease?
options: Father had a myocardial infarction at 55
Paternal grandfather had a myocardial infarction at 50
Mother was diagnosed with angina at 72
Uncle needed coronary bypass surgery at 48
Older brother had a myocardial infarction at 64
questions.explanation: The history counts when a **first-degree** relative was affected **before 60**. Only his father meets both conditions.
whyNot: A grandparent is not a first-degree relative.
First-degree, but affected well after 60.
An uncle is not a first-degree relative.
First-degree, but affected after 60.

questions.leadIn: Pick the best match from the list for each case below. Any option can serve several cases, or none at all.

items.stem: A 24-year-old man has a soft, blowing murmur straight after S2, heard best along the left sternal border with him sitting forward and breath held out. Which pulse finding would you expect when you lift his arm above his head?
items.explanation: That diastolic murmur is **aortic regurgitation**; a large stroke volume with diastolic run-off gives a collapsing (water-hammer) pulse.

items.stem: An 81-year-old woman with heart failure has nausea after her digoxin dose was increased. Each normal beat is followed closely by an early, weaker beat.
items.explanation: An ectopic after every sinus beat is bigeminus, classically from **digoxin toxicity**.

items.stem: A 50-year-old woman with lung cancer becomes breathless and hypotensive. Her JVP is very high and her heart sounds are quiet. Which pulse sign would you look for?
items.explanation: Step 1: hypotension, raised JVP and quiet heart sounds suggest **tamponade**. Step 2: tamponade exaggerates the inspiratory fall in systolic BP (over 10 mmHg), i.e. pulsus paradoxus.

questions.stem: A 77-year-old man on doxazosin reports dizziness when he gets up. His lying blood pressure is 150/84 mmHg. Five readings taken at different times after he stands are listed.
questions.leadIn: Which standing reading meets Davidson's definition of postural hypotension?
questions.explanation: Davidson's definition is a fall of **more than 20 mmHg systolic or more than 10 mmHg diastolic**. 150 → 128 is a 22 mmHg systolic fall.
whyNot: Falls of 12 systolic and 4 diastolic are below both cut-offs.
A 16 mmHg systolic fall meets Talley's 15 mmHg threshold but not Davidson's 20 mmHg.
Falls of 4 and 6 mmHg are trivial.
Falls of 10 systolic and 8 diastolic do not exceed either cut-off.

questions.leadIn: Pick the best match from the list for each case below. Any option can serve several cases, or none at all.
options: Steep y descent with a high JVP

items.stem: A 38-year-old man who injects drugs has fever and a pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge that gets louder on inspiration. His liver is enlarged and pulsatile. Which JVP feature would you expect to see rising with each ventricular systole?
items.explanation: Step 1: a right-sided pansystolic murmur with a **pulsatile liver** is tricuspid regurgitation. Step 2: TR produces giant **v waves** in the JVP.

items.stem: A 59-year-old man has had three days of profuse vomiting and diarrhoea. His blood pressure is 92/60 mmHg and his mouth is dry.
items.explanation: Hypovolaemia lowers right atrial pressure, so the JVP is **low** and often not visible at 45°.

items.stem: A 55-year-old man had tuberculous pericarditis two years ago. He now has ascites and ankle oedema. You watch his neck while he breathes in deeply. What happens to his JVP during inspiration?
items.explanation: Constrictive pericarditis stops the right heart filling more on inspiration, so the JVP **rises** on inspiration (Kussmaul's sign) instead of falling.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man has had hypertension for 20 years. His ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy.
questions.leadIn: Which apex beat would you expect?
questions.explanation: Hypertension is a **pressure load**: the LV thickens rather than dilates, giving a discrete, sustained, heaving apex that is not displaced.
whyNot: A displaced thrusting apex is volume overload (MR, AR, dilated cardiomyopathy).
A tapping apex is the palpable S1 of mitral stenosis.
A double impulse suggests HCM.
Dyskinesia follows anterior MI or LV aneurysm.

questions.leadIn: Pick the best match from the list for each case below. Any option can serve several cases, or none at all.
options: Wide but variable splitting of S2

items.stem: A healthy 27-year-old woman is 32 weeks pregnant. A low-pitched extra sound is heard just after S2. There is no murmur, her JVP is normal and she is not breathless.
items.explanation: S3 is common in the **young and in pregnancy**. With no heart failure signs, it is physiological.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman has a secundum atrial septal defect on echocardiography. What happens to her second heart sound?
items.explanation: An ASD gives **fixed wide splitting** of S2 that does not change with breathing.

items.stem: A 71-year-old man's ECG shows left bundle branch block. The two parts of S2 move apart when he breathes out.
items.explanation: LBBB delays LV emptying, so A2 comes after P2 and the split widens in expiration: **reversed splitting**.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman with long-standing hypertension has been in permanent atrial fibrillation for two years.
questions.leadIn: Which auscultatory finding cannot be present?
questions.explanation: S4 is produced by atrial contraction into a stiff ventricle. In AF there is **no coordinated atrial contraction**, so S4 is absent.
whyNot: S3 comes from rapid early ventricular filling and can occur in AF.
MR or TR murmurs do not depend on atrial contraction.
An opening snap of MS can be heard in AF, which often accompanies MS.
AR murmurs do not depend on atrial contraction.

questions.leadIn: Pick the best match from the list for each case below. Any option can serve several cases, or none at all.

items.stem: A 21-year-old student has a grade 2 mid-systolic murmur at the left sternal edge found at a sports medical. It does not radiate, there is no thrill, and his pulse, heart sounds and apex are normal.
items.explanation: Soft, mid-systolic, at the left sternal edge, not radiating and with an otherwise **normal heart**: the features of an innocent murmur.

items.stem: A 17-year-old footballer fainted during a match. He has an ejection systolic murmur at the left sternal edge that gets louder when he strains against a closed glottis and softer when he squats.
items.explanation: Step 1: exertional syncope in a young athlete. Step 2: the murmur **rises with Valsalva and falls with squatting**, the opposite of AS: HCM.

items.stem: A 60-year-old woman who had rheumatic fever as a child has a malar flush. A low-pitched rumble is heard at the apex with the bell when she lies on her left side.
items.explanation: A mid-diastolic rumble at the apex, heard with the bell in the **left lateral position**, plus a malar flush and rheumatic history: mitral stenosis.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman had an inferior myocardial infarction a week ago. She is now breathless and has a new murmur. It is loudest at the apex, lasts throughout systole up to S2 and radiates to the left axilla.
questions.leadIn: Which lesion is most likely?
questions.explanation: A pansystolic murmur loudest at the **apex** and radiating to the **axilla** is mitral regurgitation; here from papillary muscle damage after MI.
whyNot: AS is ejection systolic at the base, radiating to the neck.
A VSD murmur is pansystolic but harsh and loudest at the lower left sternal edge, not blowing and apical with axillary radiation.
TR is pansystolic at the lower left sternal edge, louder on inspiration.
AR is early diastolic, not pansystolic.

questions.leadIn: Pick the best match from the list for each case below. Any option can serve several cases, or none at all.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman has had severe mitral regurgitation for years and is now breathless on exertion.
items.explanation: Chronic regurgitation is a **volume load**: the LV dilates, so the apex is displaced and thrusting.

items.stem: A 69-year-old man with severe emphysema has a barrel chest. You cannot find his apex in either lateral position.
items.explanation: Hyperinflated lungs lie between the heart and the chest wall, so the apex is often **impalpable** in emphysema.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman's brother died suddenly at 19. She has an ejection systolic murmur that becomes softer when she squats.
items.explanation: Step 1: sudden family death plus a dynamic outflow murmur suggests **HCM**. Step 2: HCM gives a double apical impulse.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man had a large anterior myocardial infarction 6 months ago and echocardiography shows an LV aneurysm.
items.explanation: An aneurysmal segment bulges out of step with the rest of the ventricle: a displaced, **dyskinetic** apex.

questions.stem: You are trying to decide whether a pulsation in the right side of the neck is the JVP or the carotid artery.
questions.leadIn: Which feature indicates that it is venous?
options: A single peak with each heartbeat
It rises when you press firmly on the abdomen
It is unchanged when the patient sits upright
It persists despite light pressure at the root of the neck
questions.explanation: Abdominal pressure pushes blood towards the right heart and **raises the JVP**. The venous pulse also has two peaks, falls on inspiration, varies with posture, is hard to feel and is abolished by light pressure.
whyNot: A single peak is arterial; the JVP has two peaks in sinus rhythm.
The JVP is barely palpable; an easily felt pulse is arterial.
The JVP changes with posture; an unchanged pulsation is arterial.
Light pressure obliterates the venous pulse; persistence suggests the carotid.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman with COPD is increasingly breathless. She sleeps on one pillow, has never woken at night short of breath and has no ankle swelling.
questions.leadIn: What does the absence of orthopnoea suggest?
options: Left ventricular failure is very unlikely to explain her breathlessness
Right ventricular failure is very likely
Pulmonary oedema is present but mild
questions.explanation: Orthopnoea reflects redistribution of pulmonary oedema when lying flat. Its **absence** carries a negative LR of 0.047 for LV failure, making LVF very unlikely.
whyNot: Orthopnoea is a left-sided feature; its absence says nothing in favour of RV failure.
Pulmonary oedema typically causes orthopnoea; its absence argues against it.
Nothing in the history points to constriction.
The absence of orthopnoea does not identify a cause; it only argues against LVF.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman is breathless after a viral illness. Her systolic blood pressure falls by 18 mmHg each time she breathes in.
questions.leadIn: What is this sign called?
questions.explanation: A normal inspiratory fall in systolic BP is under 10 mmHg. A fall of **more than 10 mmHg** is pulsus paradoxus, here suggesting a pericardial effusion with tamponade.
whyNot: Alternans is beat-to-beat alternation of strong and weak beats in severe LV failure.
Kussmaul's sign is a rise in the JVP on inspiration, not a fall in BP.
Bisferiens is a double systolic peak in mixed aortic valve disease or HCM.
Sinus arrhythmia is a normal rise in heart rate on inspiration, not a BP change.

questions.stem: A systolic murmur at the left sternal edge is loud and accompanied by a thrill you can feel with your palm. It is not audible with the stethoscope lifted off the chest.
questions.leadIn: Using Davidson's scale, what grade is this murmur?
questions.explanation: Davidson grades a **loud murmur with a thrill** as grade 4. Grade 5 is very loud; grade 6 is heard without the stethoscope on the chest.
whyNot: Grade 2 is soft, with no thrill.
Grade 3 is moderate, with no thrill.
Grade 5 is very loud; this murmur is only described as loud.
Grade 6 is audible with the stethoscope off the chest, which this murmur is not.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old man has had 40 minutes of central chest pressure. You want to know which history feature most raises the likelihood that this is an acute coronary syndrome.
questions.leadIn: Which feature has the highest positive likelihood ratio for ACS?
options: Radiation to the right arm or shoulder
questions.explanation: Step 1: recall the likelihood ratios. Highest is spread to the right arm or shoulder (4.7), then both arms (4.1); the left arm is only 2.3, and sweating, vomiting and a pressing quality are all 2.0 or less. Step 2: the highest LR+ is radiation to the **right** arm. Remember: right or both arms beats the "classic" left arm.
whyNot: Left-arm radiation (LR+ 2.3) is less discriminating than right-arm radiation.
Sweating has an LR+ of 2.0.
A pressure feeling barely shifts the probability (LR+ 1.3).
Nausea or vomiting has an LR+ of 1.9.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman reports a "fluttering" heartbeat. Her radial pulse is irregular in both timing and volume, and it stays irregular after she walks up and down the ward. The apical rate is 132/min but only 104/min can be counted at the wrist.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely rhythm?
questions.explanation: Step 1: irregular in **time and volume** = irregularly irregular. Step 2: ectopics usually settle with exercise, but this rhythm **stays irregular** after exertion. Step 3: the **pulse deficit** (apex faster than radial) happens because short-filled beats do not reach the wrist. Together: atrial fibrillation.
whyNot: Ectopic beats can cause a pulse deficit, but the irregularity usually vanishes with exercise.
Sinus arrhythmia is a regular pattern linked to breathing, with no pulse deficit.
Flutter with 2:1 block is regular at about 150/min.
SVT is fast and regular.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man has a blood pressure of 168/96 mmHg in his right arm. When you feel his right radial and right femoral pulses together, the femoral pulse is weaker and arrives later.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Step 1: hypertension in a **young** patient should trigger a search for secondary causes. Step 2: a delayed, weak femoral pulse (**radiofemoral delay**) means obstruction distal to the arm arteries. Step 3: that combination is coarctation; leg BP would also be lower instead of the usual 20 mmHg higher.
whyNot: Subclavian stenosis causes inequality between the two radial pulses, not radiofemoral delay.
Dissection presents with severe tearing pain and unequal arm pulses.
AS gives a slow-rising pulse in all arteries, not a delay between arm and leg.
Essential hypertension does not delay the femoral pulse, and a young age makes a secondary cause likelier.

questions.leadIn: Pick the best match from the list for each case below. Any option can serve several cases, or none at all.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man notices that his heart "stops, then gives a big thump" when he lies in bed at night. He is otherwise well and the feeling lasts a second.
items.explanation: A pause followed by a single forceful beat is the typical description of **ectopic beats**.

items.stem: A 67-year-old man with a large anterior MI three years ago and heart failure has sudden rapid regular palpitations followed by collapse.
items.explanation: Fast palpitations with **syncope** in someone with structural heart disease and **previous heart failure** suggest VT.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman has lost 6 kg despite a good appetite and cannot stand warm rooms. She feels a constant, regular pounding heartbeat at about 110/min.
items.explanation: Step 1: continuous, regular pounding at 90–120/min = a **hyperdynamic** sinus tachycardia. Step 2: weight loss and heat intolerance point to thyrotoxicosis as the cause.

items.stem: An 18-year-old man is noted to have a heart rate that speeds up each time he breathes in and slows as he breathes out. He has no symptoms.
items.explanation: A rate that rises on inspiration in a healthy young person is **sinus arrhythmia**, a normal finding.

questions.theme: Bedside manoeuvres in the cardiovascular examination
questions.leadIn: Pick the most useful bedside manoeuvre for each situation below. Any option can serve several situations, or none at all.
options: Bell at the apex with the patient turned onto the left side
Diaphragm at the left sternal edge, patient sitting forward in held expiration
Light pressure over the root of the neck
Raising the arm above the heart while feeling the pulse

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman has a malar flush and a loud S1. You want to bring out a suspected mid-diastolic rumble.
items.explanation: The MS rumble is **low-pitched** and apical, so use the bell at the apex with the patient on the left side.

items.stem: A 46-year-old man has a wide pulse pressure. You want to hear a suspected soft early diastolic murmur.
items.explanation: A wide pulse pressure suggests **aortic regurgitation**; its soft high-pitched murmur is best heard with the diaphragm, sitting forward in held expiration.

items.stem: A 40-year-old woman has a pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge. You want to know whether it comes from the tricuspid valve.
items.explanation: Right-sided murmurs get **louder on inspiration** because venous return to the right heart increases.

items.stem: A healthy 9-year-old has a soft continuous murmur in the right supraclavicular fossa.
items.explanation: A **venous hum** disappears with light pressure over the neck veins, confirming it is benign.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy has blue lips and tongue and finger clubbing. He squats after running.
questions.leadIn: Which condition most likely explains his central cyanosis?
questions.explanation: Central cyanosis with clubbing in a child points to a **right-to-left shunt**; Fallot's tetralogy is the classic cause.
whyNot: An ASD is a left-to-right shunt and does not cause central cyanosis.
A small VSD is a left-to-right shunt and does not cause central cyanosis.
Raynaud's causes peripheral, not central, cyanosis.
Cold causes peripheral cyanosis from vasoconstriction; the tongue stays pink.

questions.stem: An 80-year-old woman was started on prazosin for hypertension last week. Since then she has fainted twice, each time within a minute of getting out of bed.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely mechanism of her syncope?
questions.explanation: Syncope **on standing** after starting an α-blocker such as prazosin is drug-induced postural hypotension; drugs are its commonest cause.
whyNot: Prazosin is not a QT-prolonging drug; examples are sotalol, amiodarone and macrolides.
Bradycardia is caused by β-blockers, verapamil, diltiazem and digoxin, not prazosin.
Stokes–Adams attacks occur without warning, regardless of posture.
Vasovagal syncope usually has an emotional trigger and a prodrome, typically in young people.

questions.theme: Breathlessness and swelling: reading the history
questions.leadIn: Pick the best match from the list for each case below. Any option can serve several cases, or none at all.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man now sleeps on four pillows. Twice this week he woke at 2 am fighting for breath, sat on the edge of the bed and opened the window until it settled.
items.explanation: Orthopnoea plus **PND** (waking gasping, sitting up, relief over minutes) is the history of LV failure.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman notices that her eyelids and face are puffy when she wakes, and her ankles swell later in the day. Her urine is frothy.
items.explanation: Cardiac oedema is dependent and does not start in the face. **Facial puffiness** with frothy urine suggests nephrotic syndrome.

items.stem: A 66-year-old woman started amlodipine a month ago for hypertension. Both ankles are now swollen. She is not breathless, her JVP is not raised and her chest is clear.
items.explanation: Step 1: symmetrical ankle swelling without signs of heart failure. Step 2: a **calcium-channel blocker** started just before it is the likely cause.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man collapses in a supermarket. A witness says he complained of a strange smell, then fell, and his limbs jerked for about two minutes. He had bitten his tongue and remained confused for half an hour afterwards.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: An **aura** (odd smell), prolonged jerking, **tongue biting** and a long period of confusion afterwards point to a seizure rather than syncope.
whyNot: Vasovagal syncope has a prodrome of nausea and sweating with quick recovery and no prolonged confusion.
Stokes–Adams attacks give no warning and recovery is rapid with flushing; a long post-event confusion is not expected.
Postural hypotension happens on standing, with brief loss of consciousness and rapid recovery.
AS causes syncope on exertion, with no aura and quick recovery.

questions.stem: A medical student is asked to describe the normal position of the apex beat in an adult.
questions.leadIn: Which answer matches Davidson's description?
options: 5th or 6th intercostal space at the mid-clavicular line
4th intercostal space at the anterior axillary line
2nd left intercostal space at the sternal edge
5th intercostal space at the left sternal edge
7th intercostal space at the mid-axillary line
questions.explanation: Davidson places the normal apex in the **5th or 6th intercostal space at the mid-clavicular line**. Lateral or downward displacement suggests LV dilatation.
whyNot: The anterior axillary line is too lateral; this suggests displacement.
This is the pulmonary area.
The lower left sternal edge is the tricuspid area.
This is a displaced apex, as in LV dilatation.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man stopped smoking after 30 pack-years. He asks how long it will take for his risk of a heart attack to fall to that of someone who never smoked.
questions.leadIn: What is the best answer?
options: It never falls to that level
questions.explanation: The risk of MI falls to never-smoker levels after about **2 years**. The risk of developing angina takes about 10 years to approach that of non-smokers.
whyNot: Six months is too short.
Five years is longer than needed for MI risk.
Ten years applies to angina risk, not MI.
MI risk does return to never-smoker levels.

ospe.identify: Splinter haemorrhages: thin dark lines running along the long axis of the nail. Think infective endocarditis (though most are traumatic).
Janeway lesion: painless flat red macule on the palm or finger pulp, a sign of infective endocarditis (Osler's nodes, by contrast, are tender).
Tuboeruptive xanthomata over the knee: yellow nodules at pressure points, typical of type III hyperlipidaemia.
Xanthelasmata: yellow plaques on the eyelids; may be normal or reflect type II/III hyperlipidaemia.
Finger clubbing: loss of the nail-fold angle and increased phalangeal depth ratio. Cardiac causes are cyanotic congenital heart disease and infective endocarditis.
Marfan's habitus: tall, long limbs, arachnodactyly, pectus excavatum, kyphosis. Listen for aortic regurgitation.
JVP waveform: name the a, c and v waves and the x and y descents, and time them against S1 and S2.
Murmur timing diagram: identify pansystolic (MR, TR, VSD), ejection systolic (AS), late systolic with click (MVP), early diastolic (AR) and mid-diastolic with opening snap (MS).
